project_comments.note: Cross-cutting observation: Two correctness bugs were discovered and fixed in ClassifyChanges during WP-002 integration testing — not during WP-001 isolated unit testing. This underscores that the six-step classification pipeline requires end-to-end scenario coverage to validate step interactions (replacement counter, dependent attribution range). Future plans adding similar multi-step classification logic should include integration-level tests as part of the implementation WP, not deferred to a follow-on WP.

outcome_summary: Replaced the brittle position-based diff heuristics in DiffService and FileService with a mathematically precise LCS pipeline: a custom ComputeLcs method identifies the stable spine of mods, and a new six-step ClassifyChanges method classifies every change as Moved, Replaced, Inserted, Added, Removed, or a dependent shift. All 3 work packages completed with zero rework cycles, all 11 functional acceptance criteria met, and the IReadOnlyList<DiffLineModel> output contract and all consumer code are unchanged. Two integration-level correctness bugs (replacement counter over-increment and greedy causal attribution) were discovered and fixed during WP-002, and the legacy DetectReplacements and DetectAndAssignDependentChanges methods were fully removed.
project_summary: Replace the brittle position-based diff heuristics in DiffService and FileService with a Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) based pipeline. The LCS alignment identifies the stable spine of mods that maintained their relative order, providing a mathematically precise foundation for change classification, replacement detection, and dependent-change attribution. The refactor consolidates the two-layer diff system into a single coherent pipeline while preserving the exact output contract and all existing consumer behavior.
